summary: Briefly describes how the Augmentation Research Center at SRI conceptualized and used graphics terminals. Everything described had been operational for months. Attention had centered on displaying text, with pictures next.

eli5.summary: A tour of how one lab thinks about screens and what they put on them. Mostly words so far, but pictures are next.

subtitle: How the Augmentation Research Center put graphics displays to work.

tldr.problem: Graphics terminals need to be part of timesharing systems in a natural way, not requiring special privileges or complex protocols.
tldr.mechanism: ARC organized screen content into rectangular display areas that programs allocate and manage like open files, each with its own strings, positioning, font and size. The NLS subsystem formats text for different output devices using pluggable post-processors.
tldr.outcome: Users could view and edit multiple files side-by-side, with the same application code working on teletype or graphics terminals.

today: RFC 191 describes the state of graphics display design at ARC in July 1971, focusing on text display. The document notes that the lab was about to turn attention to pictorial displays and vector graphics.

sections.title: Display Areas as a Programming Model
sections.content: RFC 191 describes how the Augmentation Research Center at Stanford Research Institute conceptualized and used graphics terminals in the early 1970s. The key innovation was thinking of the display as a collection of rectangular display areas that programs allocate dynamically. A program requests an area, specifying its position on the screen and the maximum number of text strings it will contain. The operating system returns an identifier which the program uses to manipulate the area and its strings. Each string has its own position, character size, font (italic, underline, blinking), and can be moved, redrawn or deleted independently. This model treats a graphics display like a file that a program can write to, with fine-grained control over what appears where.
sections.eli5: Think of the screen as a cork board. A program asks for a rectangle on the board. Then it can pin words anywhere in that rectangle, change their size or style, or unpin them, without affecting other words.

sections.title: Teletype and Display Modes
sections.content: The system supports two display modes. In display mode, the screen shows the allocated display areas and their content. In teletype simulation mode, the screen shows the last lines of text output as if on a teletype, and user-owned display areas are suppressed. Programs can switch between modes under control. The cursor position is input with every character in display mode, allowing pointing-device interaction. This design lets the same NLS application program work on both a teletype and a graphics display: when switched to teletype mode, the program sees coordinates padded with zeros, and when in display mode, it sees real coordinates from the pointing device.
sections.eli5: The screen can look like a fancy editor with boxes and mouse, or like an old-style line printer. Switching between them is just a command.

sections.title: NLS Implementation and Format Independence
sections.content: The NLS subsystem at ARC uses display area formatters that assume a 64K by 64K addressable display, several character sizes and fonts, and 7-bit ASCII. The formatter first formats content logically, then passes the result to a post-processor specialized for the target device: a display area, a teletype, a printer, or microfilm. NLS also lets users select command arguments by pointing at text on the screen, mapping cursor coordinates through a data structure that describes the current display image. Multiple text areas in NLS allow users to split the file-viewing area vertically or horizontally, viewing and editing multiple files at once.
sections.eli5: The program thinks of text as a 64K by 64K space. A translator then squeezes it onto whatever is being used: a screen box, a printer page, or microfiche.

references.text: Deutsch, P., "DEC PDP-10 -- IMLAC COMMUNICATION SYSTEM", RFC 190, July 1971.
